description: Hi! I'm a student from TMUC FSD interested in AI, coding, and solving real-world problems using NASA open data. . We are a beginner-friendly team and no expert-level skills are required, just enthusiasm and a willingness to learn! We are looking for teammates with skills in: - Programming (Python / web development),UI/UX or graphic design.If you are creative, committed, and ready to give 2 days to build something exciting, join us!
summary:
LUNARA is a mobile strategy game for Android and iOS that puts young players in command of
an outpost near the Moon’s south pole. Players choose a crew of 2 to 6 and a mission of 15, 30
or 45 days. They then build and upgrade eight facilities, from solar farms and oxygen generators
to a greenhouse and a radiation shelter, while balancing oxygen, water, food, power, fuel and
building materials. Sunlight rises and falls through the Moon’s 29.5-day cycle, power runs short,
and emergencies such as solar storms, water leaks and micrometeorite strikes force hard
choices, each explained with the real science behind it. A Learning Center shows live NASA
space-weather data from DONKI and photos from the NASA Image and Video Library. At the
end, a transparent 100-point mission report shows exactly how every decision affected the result.
LUNARA turns the trade-offs behind real lunar missions into decisions kids can make, and learn
from.
details:
What it does

LUNARA is an educational space-mission strategy game. The player is the commander of a new

outpost on a sunlit crater rim near the lunar south pole. Their job is to keep the crew alive and

healthy until the mission ends, and they learn along the way that every resource on the Moon is

limited and every choice has a cost.

How it works

1. Plan the mission: choose a difficulty (Beginner, Intermediate or Expert), a crew size (2–6)

and a mission length (15, 30 or 45 days).2. Build the base: there are eight buildings, each with three levels: Solar Farm, Battery

Storage, Oxygen Generator, Water Recycler, Hydroponic Greenhouse, Radiation Shelter,

Medical Bay and Research Laboratory. Each one costs materials (and sometimes power,

fuel or water), takes days to build, and uses power every day.

3. Choose an operations plan: Standard, Science push (more research, but more fuel use and

radiation exposure) or Conservation (saves power, but crew morale drops).

4. End the day: the crew use oxygen, water and food. Solar output follows a sunlight dial with

a 7-day outlook, and batteries carry the base through dim periods. When power runs short,

life support gets it first, before the greenhouse and lab. Crew health and morale respond to

shortages, radiation and medical care. Cargo landers arrive every 10 days if the link to

Earth is working.

5. Face emergencies: from day 3, one of eight emergencies may strike: solar storm, oxygen

generator malfunction, water leak, power shortage, food shortage, dust damage,

communication loss or micrometeorite impact. Each offers three choices rated optimal,

acceptable or risky. Some choices need the right building (you can only shelter from a solar

storm if you built the shelter), and risky choices can backfire. A “Why does this happen?”

panel explains the real science behind each emergency.

6. Read the mission report: a 100-point score shows exactly where every point came from.

Days survived count for 15, crew survival 15, objectives 25, crew wellbeing 15, emergency

decisions 15, resource efficiency 10 and science 5.

Objectives give the mission a goal: survive to the end, keep oxygen and water reserves, build a

greenhouse, build a radiation shelter, reach a research target, handle emergencies well, keep the

crew healthy, and save enough fuel for the trip home.

Designed for young players

• Plain-language explanations for every building, emergency and topic.• Status shown with numbers and words as well as colour, plus screen-reader labels.

• Works offline and saves progress on the device. No account and no backend.

What we hope to achieve

We want kids to feel what mission control is like: making hard choices with limited resources and

learning why things went right or wrong. Next steps: unlock the Mars mission (already defined in

the game engine), connect live NASA space-weather alerts to in-game events, add a classroom

mode, and translate the game, starting with Urdu.

Tools and technologies

Expo SDK 58, React Native 0.88, TypeScript, Expo Router, NativeWind 4 (Tailwind CSS 3),

React Native Reanimated, React Native SVG, Expo Image, Lucide icons, AsyncStorage and Jest.

There are 39 automated tests, including full 15-, 30- and 45-day playthroughs on every difficulty.

Tested on iPhone with Expo Go (SDK 58).
